utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours. IT-95-16-T. The Prosector versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Before we resume the examination-in-chief by Counsel Susak. I would like to ask the Prosecutor whether they have any news. Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. In order to answer Mr. Susak's question, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber of the fact that on June 30th, 1998, among other documents which were handed over to the Defence in application of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a document bearing my signature, as well as Mr. Moskowitz's signature, was handed over to the Defence. It was a document that was a part of number of exculpatory documents. Mr. Susak yesterday asked us who was this woman, this woman who is mentioned in this document. We did specify that it was an unidentified woman whom we were talking about. As for the witness who mentions the presence of that woman, it is a witness that an investigator of the Tribunal had a discussion with, but this witness did not give any official statement. We thought it was not necessary to take a statement from this witness. We did not think it was necessary to have him come before the Court. So the only elements of information we have are those which were handed over to Mr. Susak. We thought that these elements -- Mr. Susak could lead any inquiry he would like to lead. This is what I have to say on this first issue. I don't know if you have any questions for me, Your Honours. I will try to answer them if you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Susak, any comments you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have some comments, because I don't know who this person is. Is it really a person, Mirsad Omserovic, or is this a person named differently? It seems that Omserovic, Mirsad is a man, that he is a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I've understood you well, the Prosecution has no other elements of information he can give you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can give to you the document which was handed over to Mr. Susak. I think it's quite clear. We do mention Mirsad Omserovic. This man had a short conversation with an investigator from our team. He gave an unofficial statement, an unsigned statement to the Tribunal's investigator, and this unofficial statement appears in total in this document. This potential witness, Mr. Mirsad Omserovic, does mention an unidentified woman of Croatian nationality, and this woman is said to have brought some sugar and some bread to some people. Who is that woman? We don't know. We don't have any further information on that woman. There is nothing else we can tell Mr. Susak about this woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Terrier, do you, for example, have the address of Mr. Mirsad Omserovic, because maybe this would help Mr. Susak. I think this witness is from Muslim origin, so Mr. Susak through his investigators could try to contact the witness and try to have from this witness the name of the woman mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't have the address of the witness in my documents, but it is one of the neighbours of the accused, and he lived in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Susak, does that help you at all? I think it might help you to identify the person. Maybe this could enable you to contact her through your investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think, I don't know for what reason, a different surname was cited, so it's not Mirsad Omserovic, it's another person who was an officer in the BiH Army. So it's mysterious, why wasn't it indicated that this was an officer of the BiH Army. And the correct name, because if this were correct, then the indictment against Drago Josipovic is going to be brought into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand it at all, what is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you have any comment you would like to add, Mr. Susak? What are you aiming at?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, a witness of the Court talked about this person in her testimony. She said it was Mirsad Omserovic. He was an officer of the BiH Army. He was that then and he is that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We feel that we are satisfied with the explanation given by the Prosecutor, and we should not waste time. I think it is for Counsel Susak now to look into this matter. The Prosecutor, to the best of my knowledge, has passed over, handed to him all the information he had available, so now we can move onto a second issue to be discussed with the Prosecutor this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As far as the reports from expert witnesses, reports which have been given to us, I would first of all like to mention the report written by a ballistics expert whose name is Damir Catipovic. I hope I did not mispronounce his name. This expert report was given to us by Mr. Radovic and by Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, and it describes the characteristics of a particular weapon, a Slovene weapon called MGV. If this expert is an expert as provided for by Rule 94 bis of the Rules, then of course we do accept this report and we have no intention to call this witness in order to cross-examine him. That is not our intention. But I do want to specify that the name of this expert does not appear, unless I am mistaken, on the last list of witnesses who was given to us, witnesses of Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac and Mr. Radovic, but his name appears on other witness lists. But as an expert under Rule 94 bis, we do accept the report I have just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to Mr. Radovic. Is it an expert as provided for by Rule 94 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had this testimony at the time when the Dutch police expert knew the technical characteristics of the MGV rifle, because what our expert witness wrote completely agrees with what the Dutch expert, the Dutch police expert had said. So if the Prosecution agrees for this to stay as it is, for it just to be read, I think this would be suitable. So practically everything that he said in his expert testimony is acceptable. It's beyond doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I completely agree with what Mr. Radovic has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. If I've understood you well, you told us that the name of this expert appears on the list of witnesses that should come before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. The Defence counsel of Vlatko Kupreskic have asked this witness to give a statement and another witness also was contacted by the Defence counsels to carry out both medical expertise and a ballistics expertise. But we are not talking here about Mr. Radovic or Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, we are talking here of Mr. Par and Mr. Krajina. As far as this expertise is concerned, then we would not accept it under Rule 94 bis. We would like to have the opportunity to cross-examine these two expert witnesses. Furthermore, we were handed a report written by a certain Mr. Kesic, who seems to be a geometry expert. We are not going to accept this report under the provisions of Rule 94 bis. We do want to cross-examine this witness. The same applies to the expert opinion given to us by the Defence counsels of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. This written expert report was written by Mr. Wagenaar, a Dutch citizen. Lastly, there is a slight problem. On the list of witnesses given to us by the Defence counsel of Vlatko Kupreskic, we found the name of Vjenceslav Ilic, who is a judge from the Bosnian Supreme Court. We have no information, no further information on what this witness is going to testify about. What we were given are legal decisions which do not tell us anything about what the witness is likely to say. We have asked for additional information, but we have received nothing to this day. If this Supreme Court judge wishes to give some information to the Trial Chamber on the legal principles that apply today in Bosnia, then of course we can accept this as an expert opinion, and under the rules -- and under the disposition of Rule 49 bis, but we do need further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier. Yes, Mr. Krajina, I remember that you had already told us a few things about this witness expert. It's a judge, I think he is the presiding judge of a Supreme Court and he was supposed to give us some comments on a legal decision which was given to us. So it's not really an expert witness, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Par, would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If you permit me, I would like to explain this in brief, even though we already discussed this sufficiently. This is the testimony of the President of the Supreme Court who we asked to appear before this Trial Chamber to comment on certain rulings by courts in Sarajevo which reflect the expulsion of civilian population. The President of the Court, as we mentioned earlier, we did not talk in detail with this witness, except for asking him whether he was willing to appear before the Court and to comment on the way these rulings were made. So we intended, when he appears before the Court, to tell us what the elements were of a certain act, why was a -- why was he released and for him to comment on the legal practice in this sense of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We feel this is a testimony in which we can all take part without any particular preparation, noting that the rulings that we intend to have comments upon have already been provided to the Court. So this will be testimony on the legal standpoint of the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the war crime of expulsion of civilian population. So we don't feel that we need to submit any additional materials. I think this was already accepted before by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution insists, we do want to have further information on what the witness is going to say. It's not an expert witness, from what I've understood, and the only thing we have is this legal decision, this legal ruling that was given to us. But how does that help us, and in what way is this ruling relevant to this particular case? We need further information. I don't see why it should be a problem. Why should it be difficult for the Defence counsel of Mr. Kupreskic to give us any further information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Quite. I myself would call upon Mr. Par to consider this witness as an expert witness, which would allow us to apply Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under the provisions of this Rule you could submit a written report which would be given to the Prosecution. The Prosecution would then say what its position is. Maybe these are not crucial elements to our case, so maybe we should, you know, avoid wasting any time. Maybe the best thing to do is to consider this witness as an expert witness. But if you do want to consider him only as a fact witness, then I do agree with the Prosecution's request. You do need to supply the Prosecution with further information on what this judge of the Supreme Court is likely to say. All right. Let's try to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course we will comply with the Court's request. I would only like to ask one more question regarding the objections made to the expert witness testimonies. It was stated that the Prosecutor would like to cross-examine these three expert witnesses that we proposed. My question is regarding the application of Rule 94 bis. I believe that this Rule tells us that the Prosecutor is obliged within 14 days of filing to indicate that he would like to cross-examine the expert witness. So I would like to know the standpoint of the Trial Chamber regarding the period, the deadline within which the Prosecutor needs to state whether he wishes to cross-examine. Since more than two months have gone by since we have submitted the findings, and now we hear for the first time that they are being disputed in some way. So we are interested in the position of the Trial Chamber. But I really do not wish to complicate matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, it is true that the Prosecutor has not complied with the time limit which is provided for in Rule 94 bis, 14 days. However, I think under Rule 5, we find that no material prejudice has been caused to the Defence counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic. So although, as I say, we would like to call upon the Prosecutor to comply with deadlines, I think that in this particular case no compliance does not result in any major problem, so, therefore -- and we are all under strong pressure, time pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. May I just add one thing? Maybe I am mistaken, but as far as I'm concerned, this 14-day time limit is a minimum period of time given to the Prosecution to think about his further move. We cannot go beyond this 14-day limit, but there is no maximum time limit unless the Trial Chamber wants to set a particular time limit as it just said it wants to do as far as expert reports are concerned. This is my interpretation of the Rule you're mentioning. This is not a maximum time limit, it's a minimum time limit, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I, for one, don't agree, but I think it's within 14 days of the filing of the statement the opposing party must file a notice. I think it's a strict time limit. I would not agree with you, but as I say, it is a minor problem. I mean, our Tribunal, of course, being an international Tribunal should not be fettered by legal technicalities or minor points, not on points which are crucial to a fair and expeditious trial. So, therefore, we tend to be more flexible as far as the application of Rules of Procedure concerning minor points is concerned, and this is our case. So, therefore, as I say, we know what the position of the Prosecution is. I understand only one expert witness has been accepted under Rule 94 bis, namely the expert in ballistics proposed by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac and Counsel Radovic. All the other ones must be called to court to be examined and cross-examined. Now, it is high time now to move on and to -- I will, therefore, call upon Counsel Susak to continue with his examination-in-chief of Mr. Stojak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojak?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yesterday we stopped at civilian Defence. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday what the duties of the information centre were before the war, during the war and after the war, and then you replied, but the record has something different so I repeat my question. Was the task of the information centre the same before the war, during the war and after the war?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the tasks were the same. Before the war the centre would carry out the following tasks: All mail that arrived for the civilian authorities and the secretariat for All People's Defence would go through that centre. The majority of telegrams would come in code, so these telegrams -- and we also had regular telegrams regarding the higher prices of cigarettes and oil derivatives and other general questions. This would arrive from Zenica or Sarajevo, wherever, and the telegrams pertained to everything that was of significance for the life of the population of Vitez. That was one of the tasks. The others were the civilian alarming of the population. If a natural disaster occurred, a fire or something that would threaten the civilian population, then the information would -- we would receive information from our people on the ground and then we would pass that on to the relevant bodies. We would call the fire brigade and automatically alert the population. We were also connected with the medical clinic, with the police and other organisations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Regarding the conflict of the 16th and on, mobilisation also included the civilian defence. What did the Civil Defence concretely do in the region of Vitez and the surrounding towns?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: You mean after the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. From the 16th onwards?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: The Civil Defence continued with its own activities. It still took care of the feeble population, the sick, the distribution of food for those people, but as the war was escalating and there were more and more killed people, cattle, there was realistic danger of an outbreak of disease, so the civilian defence mobilised, I think, about ten people who worked in clearing the terrain, removing the bodies of those killed and the bodies of cattle, their burial, as much as the situation permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was there an order by the commander of the Civil Defence in that period?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. When the mobilisation was announced sometime on the 16th, in the second half of that day, nothing could be done without orders. So the head of the Civil Defence command had to issue orders to his units, to the people who were directly under his command for them to carry out their tasks. So the mobilisation included those ten persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would the usher please show the witness a document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D10/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, I will tell you in brief, because this is a very brief document, you can see that this was issued by the chief of the defence office for Travnik, and it was dated April '93. Item 1 says that a number of units need to be mobilised in order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak, we need copies of these documents. Not only the Court but also the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only wanted to question the witness. I didn't manage to translate this because I found this with the witness. If the Court agrees for me to give you copies, but this needs to be translated in the briefest possible time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm afraid under our Rules we can't admit this document in evidence and it can't be used for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to use it for examination, and I would tender it as evidence later. But, all right, then I'm not going to question the witness on this today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the defence department of the municipality of Travnik issued orders on the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Are you referring to this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Among other things, I did not have to know about this order because it was not addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. Did such orders exist at that time after the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: It is only logical that they had to exist and that they had to be issued from higher levels to lower levels, so the municipality of Travnik was a higher level of authority as related to the defence department in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. So this related to the defence office of the municipality of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but a number of questions were put to the witness, answers were given to these questions but what are we talking about? Mr. Susak is referring to an order which we haven't seen, which has not been translated, which the witness himself hadn't seen before today, and he wasn't the person to whom the order was directed to. So we're not, you know, following this part of the direct-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On top of that, we don't know the subject matter of these orders. Yes. I suggest we move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday we talked about a report, and that is number 337, if I'm not mistaken, and it says that orders were issued to the Civil Defence. Today I continue along this line of questioning, that is to say, I'm asking the witness whether he knows such orders actually were issued to the Civil Defence and he answered to me that yes, they were. So regardless of this document, the witness does know about this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, are you aware of any exchanges taking place during the conflict and after the conflict, Muslims for Croats, I mean, and the other way around? May I add another thing? Do you know whether Muslims from Vitez were exchanged for Croats from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: As regards the exchange of prisoners or I don't know who, I only heard about this. If this was done, it was done at higher levels so I was not aware of it. I know that there was some kind of a commission for exchange and there were some persons who were designated. I think that the Crisis Staff dealt with it at that time, namely Mr. Ivica Santic and Mr. Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were they in charge of these activities before the conflict, during the conflict and after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I think that they were in charge of this only during the conflict, because that is what the situation required at this given point in time, because it wasn't even necessary before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Now we shall go back to your own activities. The 20th of October, 1992, do you recall this conflict, and where did this conflict take place on the 20th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: That is the first conflict between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I think it broke out in that part of Ahmici called Topola. That's what we call it. It's by the Catholic cemetery. When part of the Muslims or the Muslim units cut off all communication between Busovaca and Vitez, they stopped, I don't know, some military policeman and they disarmed him and that is when this conflict broke out, when these men returned to their unit. I don't know. They dismantled the roadblock and that's when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you were during this first conflict?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: On that day I was at home with my family, and I could not have gone out as I was encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court where your house is?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: My house is in Vitez, in the town of Vitez. That part of town which is called Mahala, in Stari Vitez, the part called Mahala. That is to say, 30 or 40 metres away from the mosque in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So that is to say in the heart of the town of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please describe the situation to us and whether you managed to get out of town during the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I could not have. I couldn't even get out of my own home. There were even some telephone provocations. These neighbours of mine thought that I was doing God knows what since I was employed in this centre. Then I received threats by telephone, but fortunately none of this was carried through because the conflict stopped and passions waned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So how did you finally manage to get to work?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I think that I went to work on the 22nd, the morning of the 22nd, when everything had calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Are you aware of the elevation or hill of Kuber?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us of what importance it is to both parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: The elevation of Kuber is on the crossroads between Busovaca, Vitez and Zenica, and it is very important because it dominates the entire valley, and from it it is easy to exercise control over the entire town of Vitez and along the communications line between Vitez and Busovaca, and it's also easy to reach Zenica from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fighting on Kuber in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I mostly heard about it and I also read reports of the civilian structures. There was sporadic fighting already on the 15th of April in Kuber, and later, of course, it intensified during the 16th and the 17th, and according to Civil Defence reports there were four persons who were killed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you know any of the persons who were killed?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew Mr. Livancic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us his first name?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I think his first name was Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I think I am. I know his nickname. I know how people called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And who did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: His father had a cafe in Santici. Well, it's a bit of an embarrassing name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This is Zeljo or Zoran?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Zeljo. Zeljo, yes, Zeljo was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And when did this fighting take place?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I told you a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But do you know about a place called Cajdrasi and what happened to the civilian population there, the civilians and army from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Are you talking about Cajdras?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: This is another place on the other side of Kuber by Veternica, at the very entrance to Zenica. So if you go through that forest, along that road, after the conflict broke out and off the MOS forces expelled the Croat civilians, women, children, they managed to pass through the village -- this road between Vrhovine and Kuber and part of them managed to get down to Vitez. Some of them were taken prisoner and others were still wandering around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. So that means that they were scattered about. Did they come along minefields as they were crossing Kuber, and how did they come across these minefields?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: These people were simply fleeing before the army, and they did not give much thought to the minefields they came across. Only afterwards they realised where they had passed through after -- after, I think, a man and a woman were killed as they were passing through a minefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So these two persons were killed in this minefield?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how the Muslims and the Croats were armed and in which ways did they receive their armaments, and was any of this a joint effort?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war people bought weapons in the black market through different channels, different connections, et cetera. After the warehouse in Slimena fell, this is near Travnik, then a lot of people got weapons. After Slimena fell, there were significant armament both of the HVO, and the Croat people and the then Territorial Defence. At that time, they were altogether, the Croats and the Muslims, and they shared the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So how did they share these weapons?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't a 50/50 sharing. I don't know how to call this. It was catch as catch can. I don't know how to call this. When a mob enters this kind of a warehouse, nobody can really exercise any kind of control, who would take what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You are a military expert of sorts, and what do you think were the intentions of the Muslims vis-a-vis Vitez and these other places? I am talking about before the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, their purposes were quite clear. They wanted to take Vitez and the surrounding villages, that is to say this central part of the state, as we would call it, this strategic part of the territory. Because they needed this territory so that they could link up. If you look at the map, before and after that, these Muslim villages were all around, Muslim towns and villages, and it was only Central Bosnia that was missing. That was the only thing they needed, Vitez, Busovaca, part of Novi Travnik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What do you think, were you sure that they would take that part of Bosnia and did they have more military men than the Croats did, in view of the fact they had refugees, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't much tension or hostility at the very outset. After all, we had lived together for many years. For example, the place where I lived, it was quite natural that we would go and visit each other, et cetera. However, these tensions mounted after various minor incidents, after Slimena fell, when people got all these weapons. After the refugees came from Krajina and Jajce, the Muslims remained in our territory, whereas Croats mainly left and went to Herzegovina and further on. They probably felt that they were stronger than we were, and that they had outnumbered us, and it is only logical that they thought that they could take this territory for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you think that they thought that they would take this part of town easily? Are you trying to say that that's the way they took Bugogno?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is probably part of their tactics, either premeditated or not. But judging by the way they attacked, it seems that they thought that they could take everything in a day or two, because that is what happened in Bugogno, the fighting didn't go on for two or three days even.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Does Muslim territory go from Travnik to Mostar? Was that an area that was held by the BiH Army, from Travnik to Mostar? Are you saying that this is the case now or earlier on?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Now. Now. The end of the war. Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, but not along communications. And if a person were to walk on foot?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you can take paths leading through forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, that's what I asked you, yes. Since you said that you were in an oasis in Vitez, do you know what the road of salvation was?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about it.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: That was a road that was built by the Muslims and Croats together. It is my impression that Croats worked on it a bit more, but never mind. It went via Novi Travnik, Pavlovica, to Gornji Vakuf, Prozor and across Mt. Vran or Cvrsnica. I'm not sure now. There were these two different roads. And it ultimately led to Tomislavgrad and Posusje. And that is the road along which food supplies were received during the Serb aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was that road cut off sometimes?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. During the first conflict also this road was immediately cut off, and this was also the case during the second conflict. I think there is a Croat village up there called Sebesic. Before they withdrew, they held part of their territory, but communications were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. Now we are going to move onto April 16th, 1993. Could you please tell the Court where you were on the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th of March -- I mean the 15th of April of '93, I was off, I wasn't on duty at the centre, so I was at my house for most of the day, because I was supposed to go to a wedding on Saturday, the 17th. I was supposed to be the best man to a friend of mine. So he came to visit me and we were talking about the preparations for the wedding, the protocol. These are our customs. And then at night, at around 8 p.m. when my shift started, I went to the centre, to the information centre to work for my regular shift, because we were working at the centre from 12.00 noon to midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So in what way did you find out that there was a conflict?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: This was on the 16th, in the early morning. There was shooting from all directions. We could hear the detonations. And then later people reported back to us. And because they were used to calling us, to ask us what was going on, that's how we found out that there was shooting, that somebody had attacked somebody, that war simply had erupted in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So the war started around in the morning before 6.00, around 5.30 a.m. So you were in the centre. So you said that your house was in the Muslim part of Vitez. Where were your children and your wife?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: My wife and my two children and my mother were at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were in Mahala. They were there for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This was under the control of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The place where we live has five Croatian houses, five houses with Croatian families. So on that morning when the war broke out, they took shelter in one house. There was seven women, nine children. And let me just recall for a minute. There were five, six men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So if one was to ask you now, okay, you are in the information centre and you are saying that you didn't know about the conflict, if you had known about it, would you have taken your family out, your wife, your children and your mother, would you have taken them out of the Muslim part of the town which was under the control of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I am asking you who wouldn't have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So if you had known, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's logical that I would have transferred them to a place where they would be safer, where there was a Croat population, because my wife comes from Stari Vitez, which is close to the church. Her parents live up there and we have relatives up there, so it's logical that I would have told them to go up there, that there will be war or I don't know what. I wouldn't wait for three days for some kind of holy apparition for them to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So what did you do and when did your wife, children and mother leave Mahala?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course I tried in all possible ways to get to them, and I couldn't get to them. So the only thing that was left to me was to go there on foot, and then, if they hadn't come out that night, that third night, the next morning, I would have gone to get them even at the cost of my own life. So after the cistern exploded in Mahala, and they didn't even know what was going on, they simply all came out into the street and they could see UNPROFOR tanks loading people into those tanks and taking them in the direction of Travnik. And since my wife could speak English a little bit, she asked one of the soldiers or officers, I don't know, this is what she told me, she told them they were Croats, they were afraid for their lives, and she was asking them to take them as far as the church in Stari Vitez, which he refused to do. And he said that they were not taking Croats. However, another soldier or officer of UNPROFOR who was just passing by, he saw that there was something wrong, he asked what was going on. And then she replied in the same way that she did to the first soldier. And then he said for them to go into one of the tanks. And they all got inside, the women and the children, and the men remained at their homes. So they all went inside the tank and they were taken up to the church in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you return to live in your house?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How far are you living from that house now?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps some 500 to 600 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So now we are talking about the 16th of April, 1993. Do you know whether the head of the Crisis Staff, Ivica Santic, who was also the mayor of Vitez, issued any kind of order about taking care of women and children and also about the clearing of terrain? So I am continuing with the questions that I already asked. Did you have any formal knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that the chief of the Crisis Staff issued an order to the headquarters of the civil defence to form a group to clear the terrain. And then, as part of their regular duties, also to take care of the feeble, meaning the women and children. And since they felt that a large number of the population could be jeopardised because of the inability to supply them with food and the required medicines or medical treatment, I think they kind of separated everybody into sections. Then at certain houses they collected numbers of people in order to carry out these tasks more efficiently. So it was difficult for a civil defence official to run from one house to another to perform his duties, because this would bring his life into danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So it was decided to deliver food to certain locations?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So this came out of the order issued by Ivica Santic?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know, since we are talking about this, do you know anything about humanitarian aid in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, before the conflict. How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid was mostly organised through two humanitarian organisations, Caritas, who worked for the Croats, Merhamet for the Muslims. There was also the Red Cross, but it mainly distributed aid through these two humanitarian organisations. But I don't exclude the possibility that Caritas distributed food to Muslims or that Merhamet gave aid to some Croats. Because it happened quite often that the Red Cross distribution would mix up the food, since Muslims don't eat pork. So then they would give this to Caritas and then it would be exchanged for oil.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This happened before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And afterwards?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, afterwards it's not really that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So, please, could you tell us how many Croats perished in Vitez, if you know this information, from the outbreak of the conflict and onwards?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: You mean how many were killed or how many were killed and wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, separately, how many were killed and how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think the information will not be precise, but approximately about 1.300 or 1.400 were killed, and almost 5.000 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know Drago Josipovic? Do you see him in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Would you please describe him, where is he sitting?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't really see him too well behind the pillar. I can see half of him. He has a moustache. Now he is smiling. He is sitting next to Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Okay. So we can note that you recognise Drago Josipovic. What kind of a person is Drago Josipovic, if you knew him from before? Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we didn't really know each other too well, but we knew each other. Vitez is a small town and we all know one another, more or less. He was a quiet family man, took care of himself and his family, probably just like all of us who lived together as neighbours with Muslims and had contacts with them. So he lived with them to the extent that the circumstances called for. And this was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Since you were in the centre of the town and in the administration of the Vitez municipality, could you tell us whether Drago Josipovic was politically active?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was he a member of any party or -- including the HDZ? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he participate in the governing bodies?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he influence any kind of decision-making in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't think he could have had any influence on that because those decisions were made at a higher level, so we just ordinary mortals didn't have much influence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When you talked about the level of decision-making, what level did you mean? You said higher levels.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, decisions were generally made at the municipal leadership level by the mayor, his deputy and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who was the mayor and who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: The structure of authority in the municipality was relative to the election results which had taken place just before that. So the mayor was Ivica Santic and his deputy or the chairman of the executive committee was Mr. Fuad Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So this was before the governing bodies separated?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So the posts were according to the results of the elections?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were five sections in the municipality, so since the Croats were a majority population in Vitez, there were two per cent more of them than Muslims, so they had three departments, and Muslims had two departments in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So during the conflict who was the mayor and who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Before the conflict the authorities divided. There was the Croat authorities and the Muslim authorities. There were two civilian police forces, two military police forces, and then simply after the conflict Muslims simply did not want to have joint government or whatever you would like to call it. They simply left those bodies, even though contacts were maintained, but not such close contacts that they had before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And then there was complete separation?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, complete separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So after this separation, who was the mayor and who was his deputy in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Ivica Santic was the mayor and then his deputy. His deputy was usually Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: One more or two questions, and then I will be through. The village guards, when were they formed and how did they operate? Were they joint guards or separate guards?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Like life in Vitez in general during the war, at the beginning it started out as joint guards, so I said that in the beginning these were self-organised groups of people or individuals who would guard their street, their surrounding few houses, neighbouring houses. So in the beginning these guards were joint by Muslims and Croats. And this went on until the first conflict broke out. After that they separated for the personal security of individuals. I don't know, they didn't trust one another any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were they formally established or --

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand. How do you mean "formally"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, how were they organised? Was there a commander of the village guards, and who appointed him, how was he elected?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I said earlier that these were self-organised groups of people. They organised themselves. They would elect their own leader, a person that they would report to. But they mostly made decisions by meeting on the street or in some room, and then they would make a joint decision. And decisions mostly pertained to the shifts, who is going to be on duty at what time, when would he be off, when would he be on duty and so on. So everything was agreed upon

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, I have no further questions. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Susak. Cross-examination by other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, just a few questions. Since you lived in Mahala, in the Muslim part of Stari Vitez, do you know which forces of the BiH Army were there, what units were these, which military units were stationed in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: You mean during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Before the conflict and during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, when the separation took place, they had appropriated the Territorial Defence and they moved their headquarters, their command to Mahala. I do not know the exact name of their formation or their unit, but approximately this was the size of a battalion, about 500 armed men. But it is certain that half of them are people who came from other places. That is to say, it wasn't only the local population that lived there, because after all, I grew up there and I know these people, but as refugees came from Krajina, from Jajce, from Eastern Bosnia, from Sanjak, they took them in, they provided some kind of accommodation to them. I don't know. At any rate, they stayed there and they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was it customary before the war to see armed Muslim soldiers in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was customary, because their headquarters was at the fire brigade building and they thought this was their own territory. These were times of war and everybody walked around with weapons and they had gravitated towards this area. That is to say, they lived there, and they also reviewed the units they had there and the kind of weapons they had, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see any such review?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you assess how many people there were at this review? I'm talking about the pre-war period.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that they ever had an entire unit there. Usually these were smaller military formations. So, for example, today they would have a platoon or a squad, these lower combat units, because it was a small area, and very often their training took place near Lasva, where there was a clearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mean training their own units?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Training their own soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In addition to the army that you said that they didn't -- you did not know what unit they belonged to, was there a civilian and a military police also in Mahala? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was a military police and there was a civilian police. When there was a separation of authority in Vitez, then they transferred all their own authorities into the fire brigade building. They belonged to the 325th Mountain Brigade, but I don't know what size it was. I don't know whether they had other units within.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you notice any trench digging in Mahala or around Mahala?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, before the second conflict broke out? Yes, yes, I managed to notice this. First of all, trenches were dug just before the outbreak of the first conflict. Of course, this was supposed to be some kind of an exercise, and as I said a few minutes ago, this was near the Lasva and in that clearing, but as soon as the conflict took place then trenches were dug near that area. I think that the area concerned is about 500 by 500 metres, this is a rough estimate of mine, and that's where trenches were dug. After the first cease-fire was signed, they camouflaged this area. They pretended to cover up these trenches but they didn't really, so they used this very cleverly in their own military operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the part of Vitez which is called Mahala, what was the approximate population there in the pre-war times, excluding the refugees?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, about 250 houses, 300 at a maximum. Well, how many people there are --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many Croat houses were there and how many Croats lived in the area of Mahala; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there were two parts and two small Croat neighbourhoods in the part near the mosque. There were eight, eight Croat houses, and the other part around the fire brigade building, I think -- yes, I think there were five Croat houses there. They lived there with their families of roughly four members per family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, what about the intensity of the fighting around Stari Vitez on the 16th of April? How long did this go on and was this heavy fighting? Were attempts made to enter Stari Vitez by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether attempts were made to enter, but I just know that one didn't dare go into the street for fear of snipers, bullets. I know that many people were killed in -- along these roads and streets that go from Mahala. As they were running in various directions quite a few people got killed or injured. I wasn't there at the time, I was at the centre, and I was wounded by a shell on the third day and I was taken to hospital, so -- so I cannot exactly describe these events, that is to say, whether the HVO units tried to enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about the intensity of the fighting around Mahala? You said there was heavy fighting in Vitez so that relates to Mahala; right?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mahala. Because most of the gunfire came from that side, that is to say, from Mahala towards the town. Within town there wasn't much -- I don't know, much shooting, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, what happened to the Croats who happened to be in Mahala between the 15th and the 16th, or on the morning of the 16th? You said that your family managed to get out with UNPROFOR. Were there any Croats who were killed?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. My grandmother, my maternal grandmother. She had been born in 1908. She died a few minutes -- a few years ago, and she spent the entire war there and she didn't want to get out. On the third day, the women went out. After the truck bomb went off, then the women got out and the men were taken prisoner, and the men told us about this afterwards, including our next door neighbour. He -- told us about it too. Mehmedovic was his name. They were staying in his basement. A military policeman told me about it later too. He came to get a young man called Dragan Pavlovic Gagalica. They had really mistreated him. They put a gun in his mouth and did all sorts of things. Anyway, they were looking for me and it boiled down to that. They were looking for me. I don't know for what reasons. This was probably only a pre-text. So these men were exchanged later on, I think 15 or 20 days later. But across the road, on the other side of the cemetery where Andzelko Miskovic lived -- my grandmother saw this. This is where her old house is. She saw it when he was killed. And after that he had -- his throat was slit and they left him by that house. Then when things calmed down, my grandmother summoned the courage to go out and drag him into an old building, a basement, we called it the Magaza, during the night, and she dug a grave for him herself during the night, and then she buried him there, and then afterwards he was exhumed and exchanged. I think he was from Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the case of a woman and her son who was a disabled person, who was in a wheelchair, from Mahala?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: That was Dragica Prkacin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Until this very day, no one knows what happened to her, and her son Vlado too. No one knows what happened to them. They lived up there near Princip, near Remiza, and it has never been proved but it is believed that they burned down in these houses, and he -- and their son Dragan was looking for her intensively and he never found them. There's another person, Vidovic. He was killed in Mahala too, or he's missing in Mahala. So I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We may probably start with the cross-examination by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Defence counsel, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My name is Michael Blaxill. I am one of the Prosecutor lawyers assigned to this case. I do just have a few questions, and I shall endeavour to keep you and the court as little time as I can. You stated, sir, that you worked in the information office, which I believe formed part of the defence office of the municipal authorities, the TO -- the HVO, rather, in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Not the Territorial Defence. It is part of the defence department. That is to say, within the defence department there were several different services, and one of these services was the centre 985.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were you -- in that role were you, in fact, in a military occupation or were you a civilian employee?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I was a civilian employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was this office a successor to what was known as the municipal ONO in the former Yugoslavia, before the break-up?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Are you talking about the defence office of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but that wasn't its name. Its name was the secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And within that office, obviously that had involvement then with the former JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Before the conflict. In the former system, in that other system, the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. So when your office started working as a defence office for the HVO, would you say it was fair to suggest you had sort of taken over the administrative and structural style of the old system?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you cannot really say that it was taken over in that sense. During the shelling, during the war operations, a lot of these files were removed and lost ultimately. So certain things to be modified. But in principle, that was it more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I believe that the HVO itself was formed in about June 1992. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Are you talking about HVO military units?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, both the civilian administration of the HVO and the HVO as a military body as well.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I really could not answer that question, whether it was in June '92 that this was established, because we were at lower levels after all, and these were people at higher levels of authority that made such decisions. But I think that the formal establishment somehow coincided with this first conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, because until then all of it was somehow shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would it be fair to suggest to you, sir, that you would have become aware of the existence of the HVO around the middle of 1992? Would that be more appropriate?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the HVO and, I don't know, some kind of war units were set up as some kind of security for -- for the Croat people in that part of the territory that we lived in, so -- so we had, as our own protection at that time, the civilian police force, and later on came this military police. At first they were shared, as I said. There was HVO military police and BH army military police. But it's very difficult to make a distinction whether it was the HVO that was set up or, I don't know, some other kind of military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stojak you were working in an information centre. Was this the sole information centre that was used by the HVO authorities in Vitez? I will say, firstly, the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, not HVO authorities, only the civilian authorities of the municipality of Vitez, because the defence office was a civilian authority, it had nothing to do with the army. And also, you asked me about this a few minutes ago, and it's not clear to me really what you're asking me, because my boss, until the first conflict, was a Muslim, Zlotrg Nedim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then I will ask you this, Mr. Stojak: You said that the defence office had nothing to do with the civilian administration, Muslim or HVO, so is it true to say that your office worked directly with the HVO military within Vitez? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. You put it the other way around. The defence office was a civilian component of government. It was not a military component of government. Defence offices belong to the civilian sector otherwise, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So did -- as a civilian body, did your office handle any materials that had relevance to the military, its establishment, its supply or its operations?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: According to the establishment rules of the former JNA, it is the defence office that at the request the military component carries out certain activities, such as mobilisation of personnel and mobilisation of needed logistics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But as regards your component of the information, I would ask you again, sir, did you handle, yourself, any military communications that passed to or from the HVO military in that area?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I want to ask you just a couple of fairly brief questions on this issue of mobilisation of persons. From your knowledge, sir, and your academic experience in the field of defence, is it a true generalisation that in the former Yugoslavia, before the conflict, basically all males of military age were liable to do JNA service? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Are you talking about the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in the former Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, is it true that subsequently people were also required essentially to be prepared to serve and protect the state? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will turn to the subject of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Are you familiar with that term and that concept, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm familiar with the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with any of the publications in what is called the Nadrodni List, official decrees of the communities, the community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I am familiar with the term "Official Gazette," whereas the official List of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, I've never seen one so I cannot say that I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I regret sir, I was probably abusing your language, which I do not speak, and it was probably my mistake. The Official Gazette is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Official Gazette. That I know, because I had the opportunity of holding copies in my hands, the former ones. However, I did not ever hold in my own hands the Official Gazette of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, so I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There is one document I would like to put to this witness, Your Honours. This document was served this morning. Copies are being made available now. It involves a number of Articles published by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, but I am referring only to Articles 3 and 4 for brevity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, do you think that this is a convenient time for a break now, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very easily. We can distribute the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked 349.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll break now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The accused entered court) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, you see a document before you, which is part of a decree on the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, which was published in November, 1992. I would ask you, sir, to look at Article 3 of that document. I think it's on the first page. If you've had an opportunity to read that, Mr. Stojak. Would you agree that that Article appears to impose a basic obligation on all the citizens of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna principally to serve in the army and then to perform all other duties for the protection and defence of the state. Would you say that is correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: (no translation) -- kept to these articles. It means, yes, this should be so in theory, but in practice it wasn't like that, because this is obviously just copied from the earlier law, and I think there was some changes, because I see under Article 4 the duty to participate in the monitoring and information service. So I would have to be aware of that. But nothing really concretely happened regarding this in my department. So I don't think that this was strictly adhered to. I can give an example, for example, in the previous army under the systemisation, it was quite usual, if a citizen was leaving the country, he had a duty to report to the police and to the defence office. So that in case of mobilisation, he could be mobilised. But during the war times nobody reported to anybody. There wasn't really that much responsibility on individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would in fact ask you briefly, in connection with Article 4, would it be correct to say that, in principle, the other work or service to the community would be only if the person had not been assigned as a primary duty to the armed forces? That appears to be the meaning of the Article? Would you agree that in principle that is so?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you please repeat your question regarding Article 4. For persons who were not mobilised, would they be subject to compulsory work duty?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That appears indeed to be what the Article says. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can't contest what it states here. It states what it states. I didn't write that down. But this wasn't like that in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, did you hear in the course of your duties, or just as a member of the community in the Vitez area, of the -- let us say the intentions and the purposes of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you as a Croat citizen, sir, never aware of any declaration that that community had been set up with the intention of political, economic and territorial, let us say, independence or autonomy?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So even something which you may or may not agree, sir, would seem a significant matter for the Croatian population of that area, that was not any form of information that you ever received?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you aware of the thing called the Vance-Owen Plan? Did you ever hear about that just as a Croatian citizen of that area, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, mostly from the media, from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you aware from those media reports that Vitez lay in a province known as province number 10 under that plan?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you therefore similarly unaware of any indications by the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna that they wished province 10 to be fully Croat controlled? That did not get through to you?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No. This is political information at a higher level, so I wouldn't really know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you not feel, sir, that such potentially important matters for the population were of interest in terms of your duties as a collector of information?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: We did not deal with such information. Mostly we dealt with those of civilian character. So let me clarify, number 988, this was an emergency telephone where ordinary citizens only on the municipality of Vitez, the territory of Vitez would call in case of danger, their personal danger, or some kind of threat to society. So these decisions of higher import were not something that I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have informed this Trial Chamber of the operation to cease weapons from the warehouse at Slimena. Mr. Stojak, do you recall who provided the greater numbers of manpower for that attack, for that operation? Was it the HVO or the local Muslim TO?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I can't say that this was the local HVO or the Territorial Defence. There were people from one and from the other, so it just kind of went in waves from moment to moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You made the assertion, sir, that of the weapons seized, there was not a 50/50 split. Could you explain that a little further, what you meant by that expression "not a 50/50 split?"

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you can't say that the TO or some HVO units, whatever have you, had captured these weapons, placed them in one location, and then according to some form of division distributed a certain amount to the Croats and a certain amount to the Muslims. It wasn't like that. Women and children went there, I don't know, people without any kind of control. It wasn't possible to control. There was complete disarray.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So indeed, sir, what you are saying to this Court, if I understand you correctly, is that there was no programmed disciplined sharing of these weapons, people just helped themselves as they could; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You have already stated that you did not have sight of military orders issued by the HVO command. I believe I am correct in saying that, sir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't have seen them. Since we are the civilian structure, the civilian component.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would have to ask you, Mr. Stojak, that although a civilian component, you were part, you say, of the defence office, that this was civilian defence, was it?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: The civil protection is one thing and the centre for information is something else. So it's a part of the defence office. It's within one unit, but it's divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Therefore, other components of the defence office were linked directly to the military; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Only in the case of mobilisation, so at the request of the military component, but they didn't have any right to interfere in the military component. This is what it states under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: All right. If I may move on, sir, to the events of April of 1993. You said you did not handle any military orders through your department, but were you aware of any instructions from HVO command about heightened readiness of HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see any signs of increased combat readiness of HVO formations in the Vitez area in the first few days of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you stated that you in fact were having a day off on the 15th of April and were at your home in Mahala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I put it to you, sir, Mr. Stojak, you clearly, I suggest, had no fears of some Muslim attack on that area of the Lasva Valley on or about the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Of course I didn't have any fear. If I didn't know that somebody was going to attack me, how could I have been afraid?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Precisely, sir. Thank you. Now, had you at that time -- sorry, I should withdraw that. You subsequently say that you believed that the Muslims wanted to attack and seize all the territory between Travnik and Mostar. Is this an opinion that you formed subsequent to those events?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't say between Travnik and Mostar. I was talking about the Lasva River Valley, about Busovaca, Vitez and Novi Travnik, and this conclusion I made after this war. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But we can be absolutely clear that you had no such fears on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I repeat that I was afraid. If I had known somebody was going to attack me, of course I would have prepared. I wouldn't have acted normally. I was actually preparing for a wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, you've mentioned the ABiH military force in Stari Vitez. I would just like to confirm, you said that generally that was a presence equivalent to, say, a platoon or a squad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said that the -- I didn't know anything about the size of the military formation, what it would be, because I didn't know their structure.
