I didn't know what was a brigade, how many people made up a brigade, but I said that there were about 500 people, men, under arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I must have misunderstood you when I noted the word. You at some point said a platoon or a squad. I must have misunderstood you, sir.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was talking about when they were having the review. Not all the men could stand up at the same -- at once. So it was logical, when they were doing the review, that they did it in smaller numbers of soldiers in such formations, from 20 to 50 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear to me, Mr. Stojak. I am obliged to you, sir. Now, you stated you were awakened early on the morning of the 16th of April at the sounds of gunfire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There was no translation. Could you please translate what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask the question again. The first thing on the 16th of April, 1993, what was the first thing you noticed that indicated that there was some kind of attack or military operation going on?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you first asked me whether I woke up, and I am answering, I couldn't have woken up because I had just worked on the nightshift. So I hadn't gone to sleep. At 5.30 a.m. we could hear detonations, shooting from all directions, and that's how I concluded that something was happening outside. And then later, through phone calls, I found out from people who were out on the terrain, who were also asking us for information, who were asking what was going on, then we saw that some kind of fighting was going on, that there was a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say you'd been on the nightshift. Had that been at your office at the defence offices premises?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this was my regular duty. I had already mentioned that we worked 12-hour shifts and then rested for 12 hours, and then worked for 12 hours again, and then we were off for 24 hours. This is how the shifts were organised at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So I can presume, and I hope I am not just stating the obvious, but I presume neither you nor your colleagues at the office had any concerns about an impending attack during that nightshift from the 15th to the 16th?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about my colleagues from the office, because physically it was separate from the information centre because they were in the municipality building. So what was happening with those people I don't know, but I could just talk about the people who were on duty with me at the centre. We didn't have any need for that. We weren't afraid, because we didn't know about it, which couldn't be said maybe for two or three hours after that on the 16th, after we found out what was happening. I wasn't so much afraid for myself as I was afraid for my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Stojak, do you know what actions were taken in Vitez by the HVO forces during that morning, the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I think -- I know that these members of the office -- are you talking about the active component, the military or the defence office?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The military, sir.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's logical that they did receive it. I think that they probably took the first strike, which is logical. So the units who were on duty that morning received the first attack, and then mobilisation took place later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And in the greater area of the town of Vitez and its municipality, were you aware, sir, of any large scale -- or subsequently aware of any large-scale rounding up of Muslim civilians by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: It's impossible that they were surrounded, the army units, meaning the Muslims, because we were the ones who were encircled during the whole of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, sir, about the internment of Muslim civilians in the cinema at Vitez, internment, detention by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: You probably consider that detainment, detention, but I connect that with the decree of Civil Defence, where there was a decree under which women, and children and feeble persons were gathered in order to have food distributed to them. So they were gathered at certain localities that I spoke about later. I don't know whether there were any detainees in the cinema house. I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about that because that was in the jurisdiction of the military command and we never left the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will ask you though, did you ever just hear about it? As a Croat of the Vitez region did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I did hear that there were some people detained there who were later exchanged for Croats, I don't know, in different areas, but this happened at some higher levels of authority. Whether there was civilian or military authorities, that I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you hear of similar internment of Muslim civilians in the Dubravica school?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you hear of wide-scale searches of Muslim apartments in the town of Vitez during the morning of the 16th of April, by HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have mentioned a number of casualties you attribute to the HVO. Is that for casualties in Vitez for the whole of the conflict, the whole of the war?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: You mean the 1,300 that I mentioned, that the figure that you mean, the killed and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the gentleman asked me from the beginning of the conflict until the end of the war, so that would be that approximate number from the very beginning of military activities, war activities, because there were also people killed in the fighting with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you know, in fact, the number of HVO casualties who died in Stari Vitez on that very day, the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that earlier. Well, I don't know whether she was killed or not. She's on the list of missing persons, Dragica Prkacin, her son Vlado. Then the late Mr. Miskovic. I know that he was killed, because this is what my grandmother told me. And then Mr. Vidovic, who is considered as missing, but the last time he was seen was in Mahala. And then I don't know about the rest. This is for the first day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And do you know the -- in fact, the number of HVO military casualties in Vitez that day, actual HVO soldiers? Please say no if you don't know, sir, please say no.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I wonder if, Your Honours, we could just show the witness document P337, Prosecution Exhibit P337. Your Honours may be interested to know I think I shall be another ten minutes or so and that will conclude cross-examination. I apologise, Your Honours, I appear to have lost the annotation of two particular names that have already been identified to this Chamber. I apologise for that. Sir, on this list I suggest, if you just look very quickly through the place and the dates, you would, in fact, find two HVO military members who were actually killed in Vitez on the 16th of April, 1993. I'm sorry to ask you to take that little extra moment to do so. It's an inefficiency on our part. On my part, I should say.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Are you referring to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think Vitez as such, the whole town of Vitez, not just Stari Vitez, the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There are names on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez. It's number 379 and 380.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged to you, Mr. President, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I could direct you a little quickly to now, courtesy of His Honour, to 379. You will see there are two names adjacent to the date. You see number 379.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Prkacin Vlado and Prkacin Dragica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm obliged to you, Your Honours. I sorry to cause you that inconvenience. Mr. Stojak, I need not trouble you to look at the document any longer. Mr. Stojak, could I ask, sir, you what, if anything, you heard upon or after the 16th of April, 1993 in respect of the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, early in the morning, we could only hear terrible shooting. I didn't hear anything specific. However, later, according to reports, when that team for assistance on the ground was formed, I heard that there were a great many victims in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Within your information centre, did you receive information because of the number of civilian victims and, therefore, mobilising assistance to those victims?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Are you talking about the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I've been talking about -- you have mentioned that you would, through your office, mobilise necessary help for the feeble or for people who suffered some kind of tragedy, disasters. I'm wondering whether your office was in any way involved as a result of what happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: I repeat once again, it was not through our centre, it was through the segment of Civil Defence. That is a segment in its own right. We only channelled information to certain places. That is to say that the teams for providing assistance were sent to the terrain, to the municipality of Vitez, as we received reports from citizens saying that such and such a thing had happened there. But we would send them there only if their lives wouldn't be jeopardised, because there was shooting all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then I will refine my question to be more accurate, sir. Did you, in fact, channel any information to any of those bodies to react to the Ahmici situation?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Specifically we heard about Ahmici, that there were many killed persons and wounded persons, and that it would be necessary to send emergency medical assistance there, and also this team for general assistance. So we only let the medical emergency team know about this, and also the Civil Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And other than that, as a matter of record, Mr. Stojak, you were not in Ahmici and did not see what happened there on the 16th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would appreciate one moment to confer, Your Honours. Thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination. I would wish to tender the document that I put in. I believe marked number 339 for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: 349. I apologise. Thank you, Mr. Stojak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection to document P349? I see no objection. It is admitted into evidence. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I shall only put two or three questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You have the decree before you; don't you?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, they took it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could the usher please give this document to the witness? Could you please open it and look at page number 9 of this decree?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please read this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy of this, and the witness is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down and tell us what particular provision of this decree you are referring to, because we can follow in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the actual title, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What does it say underneath the heading?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: "Clarified text," it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And now, could you please read the first sentence, or perhaps I can read it. "Decree on the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Official Gazette of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, number 1/92, edited version. At the meeting of the presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, on the 17th of October, 1992, and its edited version is being published." Could you please look at the last page of this decree now? Did you see that this decree was passed on the 17th of October, 1992? Did you see that? I shall repeat, page 25 --

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Article 179.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So what does this mean? This is the edited version of the decree and it was passed on the 17th of October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, it says so.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if that's what it says, that is the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Which is to say that if it was amended, edited, that is to say that it was passed before that date?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that is the general understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the introduction.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And now I have another question for you. Was this decree passed when the war was being waged against the Serbs, in your opinion? In your opinion.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: If we look at the date that it says here, and this is the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please find Article 140 now? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And now I'm going to read something else to you. "Centres for information are being established as a rule for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina - Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and if necessary in municipalities." In your opinion, does this provision relate both to Muslims and to Croats, or when the conflict occurred only between the Muslims and the Croats on the one hand and the Serbs on the other hand? So it is stated quite clearly here in Article 140.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it says here very nicely. It says for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina-Croatian, community of Herceg-Bosna and in municipalities if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: That's right. So we agree on that. So this decree on the armed forces was passed at the beginning of 1992 or mid-1992. Now I'm asking you the following: Was this decree passed before or after the conflict with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Judging by the date that is specified here, and if we accept that as the relevant date, it was before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you whether you had access to orders issued by certain commanders from the military structure.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, we did not have access.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: We did not have any contact with the military structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The Prosecutor did not show you these documents, that is to say, certain orders, although he does have them available because we have seen them, and they are strictly confidential and that is what is written on these actual documents, and in these orders it also says who was informed about these orders, and then I want to point out that this is a confidential order, and it is stated that it is sent to the head of the Crisis Staff personally or the head of the defence office?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the head of the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: These orders that were given to them did you receive copies of them? Did you know what they were all about?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you whether you were aware of this. I just want to know whether you received a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. I did not receive copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: If a copy was sent to the head of the defence office, who did that pertain to?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Then it pertained to the head of the defence office, but very often these things were only distributed. That is to say, we would send it but only in a sealed envelope. If this was strictly confidential, we would only register it, the sealed envelope, because we were the people who were in charge of that. Then we would send it to the addressee, and we had nothing to do with it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So you were not familiar with the substance?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. Of course not. We were not allowed to do that, and we were not involved in these strictly confidential matters. If the gentleman thought we were supposed know about these strictly confidential matters, they probably would have returned the order to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You also said that in your reporting centre you received information about certain phenomena. What was the telephone number of your centre, 985?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, our telephone number was 985. This was our special telephone number, our emergency telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Right. So you received reports, information on certain phenomena?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Then we had to make records of all of this, and then to register it, and we should say exactly what we did. For example, you cannot simply let a fire alarm go off without stating why you did it and what you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You mentioned number 988. Were you just confused? I mean, what is it in relation to 985?

utterances.speaker: Dragan Stojak (resumed)
utterances.text: No, no. That's just a mistake. I probably misspoke. 985 is the official telephone number for the entire territory. Until this very day this telephone number has remained unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No questions. I think there is no objection to the witness being released. Mr. Stojak, you may be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, the next witness -- are you asking any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we call Mr. Mario Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rajic, could you make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about your basic personal data, what you have done, when you were born, where you were born, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of September, 1952 in Zenica. I graduated from university. I'm an engineer of organisation of work, and I worked before the war in Vitezit, and I was in charge of preparation and control of trans service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were also a reserve officer of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also completed the reserve officers' school, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. In 1977 I left the army as a reserve officer, as a lieutenant, and since then -- or, rather, after that I was part of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war, in 1992 which post did you hold in the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: My last post?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, your last post.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: My last post in the Territorial Defence was head of Territorial Defence of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about this post of head of Territorial Defence and the general structure of the staff, how would you evaluate it?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: This was the second ranking post, after the commander. The head of the defence territorial staff would replace the other when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The commander of the staff at that time was Hakija Cenjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, at that time Hakija Cenjic was commander of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you receive any call-up papers in terms of the conflict with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I was waiting for such call-up papers, but I never received them. Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you report to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. As I was observing what was going on around me in spring, 1992, I think it was March, there were more and more attacks of the army of Republika Srpska against the town of Travnik and Turbe. I realised what the situation was and then, at my own initiative, I came to the Territorial Defence staff in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you assigned certain duties in this staff? What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: As I came to the Territorial Defence staff, my friends and colleagues who worked with me together at the Territorial Defence, we placed ourselves at the disposal of the commander, Mr. Cenjic, and we asked for him to do something specific. At that time, at the Territorial Defence headquarters, in addition to the people whom I knew and who I was with there, there were some other people whom I had not seen at Territorial Defence headquarters before. And they were in a way attached to this structure of command and they were officers in the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: These new people who appeared at headquarters, were they Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Together with me, some other Croats came to the Territorial Defence staff, that is to say Croats. Mr. Srecko Pavlovic, who was the person who was in charge of defence from chemical and biological warfare. And the staff, I am speaking in simplified terms now. Then there were other members of the Territorial Defence staff who worked there professionally, Mr. Zeljko Sajevic, Mr. Stipo Zigonjic, and then also a man in charge of logistics, Zeljo Vrebac. All the rest of them, about 20 of them there, were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you try to set up some kind of a joint Croat Muslim unit at the time?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I came for that reason to the Territorial Defence staff to give my contribution to the joint defence of our territory. After some time, when I realised what the situation was like, I proposed to Mr. Cenjic, head of the Territorial Defence staff, that I try to set up a joint unit which, according to its structure, would match the structure of the population of Vitez. We realised that this could be a sabotage and reconnaissance unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The transcript has stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you said, and then I saw that this in the transcript, that you suggested for a joint unit to be structured, a joint Muslim-Croat unit, is that right, and it would be the size of a detachment?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: The formation of a detachment -- well, it's not the size of a detachment. It would be a smaller unit which is specially trained for these purposes. This is maybe a strengthened company or, perhaps -- so I asked for this unit to be structured, and I received agreement from Mr. Cenjic to form this unit. So I got the list of the unit. I chose the conscripts. I did the proper call-up in the way it was supposed to be done, as much as was possible at the time, and I formed this reconnaissance sabotage unit in accordance with the structure of the population in the municipality of Vitez. So after reviewing the reconnaissance and sabotage unit, I got all the equipment, I replaced equipment that wasn't suitable. The review was done right in front of the warehouse where all the weapons and the materiel was stored.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you ask for these people to be armed?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. I suggested to the commander of the Territorial Defence, because at the time the unit should have been the most important impact, mobile unit, so I had some information from the commander of the staff, Cenjic, that they had received some weapons. So I requested that this be -- this unit be armed and equipped immediately, and it also be trained so that it could be ready for action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So did you receive weapons for this unit?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: No. After consultations between Mr. Cenjic and the others, I don't know exactly with whom, I received the answer that the weapons were necessary for units which were formed in the villages in the meantime, so this was besides -- outside of the TO, the Territorial Defence formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this was for the arming of the units which were structured in the villages by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So were you asked to sign any kind of special statement in order to continue working at the Territorial Defence, regardless of the fact that you were chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, after the formation of the reconnaissance sabotage unit, I didn't want to waste time, and I wanted to form a Territorial Defence unit on the same principle. Well, I was told to wait a little bit, and then after some time they came with a statement where there was a list of all the people who were at that time in the staff, including myself. And they requested us to sign a statement of loyalty to the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you condition your signing with anything?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, yes. Not only myself, but other officers of Croatian nationality asked for one sentence to be added to this list, which would state the following, that we would agree to sign this statement if the structure of the command and the army would reflect the structure of the population of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was permission granted for this sentence to be added?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cenjic said that, basically, there shouldn't be any problems regarding that, but the other Muslim officers objected over our position, and after that we were not offered the option to sign such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that you tried to form a unit which would be the size of a battalion, and it would comprise three companies, and also according to the ethnic principle, the national principle.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, yes, I wanted to continue. I wanted to form a TO unit, so it would be a kind of strengthened battalion. But after we refused to sign this, to agree, we never proceeded with my plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How were you taken away from the TO headquarters? Who did this?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, I waited for permission to start forming this TO unit, and then at one point in time our office, which was on the other end of the hall, it was separate. An officer came from the TO staff, Mr. Mirsad Varupa, and he said that I was to go home now and that they will call me from the staff when conditions are appropriate, but for now I should go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This was at what time?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: This was in '92. Yes, this was in the spring of '92.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that Vitez was shelled. Did you get any kind of call from the TO?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, after that I was at home. I am waiting for a call, you know. I am not called and I see that all kinds of things are happening around me, the army of Republika Srpska is attacking. I am the number two person, defence person of Vitez, and I am sitting at home and I don't know what to do. Then there was shelling on the 26th of April. That date is known to me for personal reasons. There was a lot of strong shelling against Vitez because the Republika Srpska army or the JNA shelled Vitez from the air. So I went to the TO headquarters, which had in the meantime moved to a yellow house in the town itself. It was the house of Baranja. So I arrived there and I placed myself at their disposal. But the attitude that was prevalent there, when I first got there, wasn't there any more. Nobody paid any attention to me, nobody asked me anything. I didn't say anything. I just kind of spent some time there. And then I went home. And this was my last encounter with the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in view of these events regarding the TO, it's obviously the intention of the TO command to isolate Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And to remove them from the TO?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's how I felt about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were also not in the HVO at the time because, obviously, you were not in favour because of your -- the fact that you belonged to the TO, so you weren't desirable to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't on one side and I wasn't on the other side. I was rejected by one side and, understandably, not accepted by the other side, because I had been a member of the TO. So then I spent some time at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But in some way did you try to carry out some defence tasks? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, realising what was happening around me, and together with all my neighbours, I also tried in some way to participate, to be present. So together with my neighbours I joined the so-called village guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You lived in Vitez, though, in the outskirts of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, I lived in the outskirts of Vitez. It's a settlement towards Krusica. It's a part of Krusica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And that's where you organised the village guard?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: No, I didn't organise it. Together with my neighbours, I joined the guard and we were keeping watch on our houses. This is what others did too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you have by way of weapons?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, our guard post, which was some 300 metres away from our homes where we kept watch over a road that led out of the forest towards our settlement, so this group of our neighbours, maybe some ten of us who were doing this task in shifts, we had an M48 rifle with seven bullets and we had a semiautomatic rifle with ten rounds, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you were doing this until the end of November of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, until a little earlier, maybe until mid-November. At the invitation of Colonel Blaskic from the headquarters, I joined up on the -- on November 1st. I went to the headquarters of the operative zone. I think that's what it was called for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I was in the operative zone from the 1st of December of 1992, and I was assigned to the position of head of operative affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What were your duties at this post?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: At that time the headquarters were being formed, so we were only getting staff from all the municipalities that were part of the operative zones. People were arriving and they were being assigned to their jobs. This was completely new compositions. So we were just learning the command structure and we were finding out about the tasks that were before us and the duties. These were people who did not have much experience in these jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is the time when the command of the operative zone was being formed, in December of '92?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what exactly were your duties? Were you on duty at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. The entire time the operatives were on duty we changed shifts and we were on duty at the headquarters of the operative zone. We did some other tasks too under orders of the chief of staff or the commander or Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was one of your duties to enable the units to move through the region of the operative zone, both Croat and Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, in that period units were going to the lines of defence against the army of Republika Srpska. So this would be the zone of responsibility towards Vlasic and Kupres. So with an internal order by Colonel Blaskic I coordinated the passage of these units to the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did this passage have to be coordinated? Who would prevent or who would stop these units?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, the orders that were issued by the commanders in charge were very clear, to enable the passage of units to the lines of defence against the army of Republika Srpska. But because of a still unsettled situation with the chain of command, some commanders at points, certain points, or local --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Commanders?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, or groups, would often meet both units on the ground. So it was my role, together with the coordinator from the headquarters of the BiH Army, to ensure passage to the units to the lines of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So there were Muslim points, checkpoints, and Croats, and there were commanders who set up these checkpoints, and then there were problems for both sides; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You stopped working at the operative zone in March of '93?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. When I arrived at the operative zone, Mr. Ljubo, who was the person in charge of structuring at the operative zone, I had a conversation with him, and he told me that I would only be temporarily at the operation zone, for about a month until the command is established, until younger people are trained in our roles. And then after that I would be demobilised, returned to the duties that I was performing before I came to the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you were demobilised in March?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In mid-March of '93 I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April a conflict broke out between Croats and Muslims. Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: On the 15th of April I was doing -- I was at my work place. I was doing my regular work. Towards the end of my working hours I picked up my monthly salary and then a friend of mine and myself, we went to a cafe, bar, where we were celebrating the birthday of a friend of ours, Milko Milkovic, because it was his birthday that day. Then at about 7 p.m. I went home. On the 16th I woke up. I was in bed on the 16th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In view of your military experience and your rank, and the fact that you were chief of the TO staff, when were you mobilised? When did they come to collect you and who came?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: The first contact was made on the 20th of April, and a member of the military police came to get me, Zlatko Nakic. He told me to get dressed, to take my equipment and to go to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the brigade, the Vitez Brigade command, that's where you were supposed to go?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What post did you then -- were you then assigned to in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, when I got to the brigade command I was assigned to be advisor for operative and teaching affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what was the situation on the 20th of April? How did you find it? The Vitez Brigade was being formed. What was the structure like?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived at the brigade, I came to a situation which was unfamiliar to me. It was chaos. Relations were completely unsettled and nobody knew their way around. The brigade was in the process of being formed. It still didn't have its own location. Nobody knew still where they were sitting and nobody knew exactly who was going to be doing what. It seemed as if everybody was just going without any kind of system or any kind of organisation. So when everybody went in one direction they all went in one direction. When they went in another direction they all went in another direction. There was no coordination there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the formation of the Vitez Brigade began in March, after the Stjepan Tomasevic was dismantled?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. This would be more the structuring of one brigade. So two brigades were supposed to be made out of one. So with the structuring of the Vitez Brigade, it practically -- this job practically was started in March.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: According to your military knowledge, how many men should be in one brigade and what are the services required by a brigade?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: According to a basic concept of a brigade, it should have a staff and units attached to the staff. That is to say, catering to the needs of the staff. Then it should have three battalions. It should have a support unit, an artillery support unit. That is to say, approximately 1.500 people or up to 1.600 people. That is what a brigade should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The unit that called itself the Viteska Brigade, how many people did it number?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Sometime in March, when it actually seceded from Stjepan Tomasevic, it had some 300 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And all of the other services that you mentioned that were required for the proper functioning of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: These other services were not established until the end of the war at all, or not properly, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you about certain things that we have partially touched upon during these proceedings. You know about this because of your rank and your experience. Tell me, what the proper way of conducting mobilisation, according to law?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, I was taught as follows and this is the way it should be: The office of defence, or the secretariat of national defence, as it was formerly known, has the following role: In the territory of the municipality of Vitez, it should gather the -- gather information and personal data about all military conscripts. That is to say, when a military unit is established and when it is established how many officers and men are needed for a specific unit, then this is -- this is the kind of information that is then sent to the defence office regarding quality and structure, and before this was called specialities, VES, and that is what a brigade required. When a brigade were to be set up, the higher command would first establish the staff of the brigade. That is to say, someone who is going to choose the others, the other members of this military unit. Then they -- they take all the men they need. I'm talking about peacetime. Then it is the defence office that sets up all these records and these lists of units, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And on the basis of these lists, as you say, then call-up papers are sent to military conscripts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. Then the defence office has to give military ID to each and every military conscript, and his special, VES, is listed there, also the code of the military unit that he belongs to and also the place where the conscript should report once he receives call-up papers. In peacetime, these call-up papers are prepared by the defence office, and then a certain unit is mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say that there should be a place where people will gather and where they will get equipment when mobilisation is proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it goes: When mobilisation is proclaimed, it can be public, secret, partial, full, et cetera, but when mobilisation is proclaimed, then messengers deliver call-up papers to military conscripts. It is the duty of each and every military conscript to report, after 24, 48 hours, or whatever time is specified, at a given place. Before that he knows which military unit he belongs to because that is what his military ID says if he has one. So while they're all reaching this point of gathering, all the equipment is there and everything else, the gear that is required by each and every military conscript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And that is where they are issued with equipment; is that right, this point where they gather?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: The commander receives them there and sets up a unit. That is to say, each and every one, depending on their own speciality, depending on the mobilisation too, and then they're issued with equipment, ammunition and perhaps even food rationings if this is not regulated otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the HVO have this kind of mobilisation point at all?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Never. I don't know whether they have it even to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence inherited the TO structure. So we did have this gathering mobilisation point that was in Gacice and also in another hamlet near Gacice, and each and every unit knew where they were supposed to go in case of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to show the witness P355 -- P335. I showed you this document earlier on, so you are aware of its contents. Certain things are mentioned here in terms of how this mobilisation was carried out. In your opinion, what was done between the 16th and the 28th of April, 1994 by the defence office? Was that a real mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: For me this is nothing. This is a poor improvisation. According to this mobilisation, I really don't think anybody could make head or tail out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can one see in any way from this document that people were gathered together at a given place, that they received call-up papers, that they received equipment and that they were sent to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I see here that people were brought in, brought in, according to this list, from certain urban areas. When I look at this list, I know approximately where each and every one of these persons live. So these people were probably picked up from their homes during this period between the 16th and the 28th, from their houses, beds, cafes, workplaces, and taken to the frontline. That is not mobilisation. People were taken away in track suits, in sports clothes, in sneakers, without equipment, without weapons, without helmets, unprepared, without military IDs, without VESs, without a mobilisation gathering point. It doesn't say here where they were taken to, to what commander, to what frontline, nothing. For me, this is nothing, in a military sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What does this text say? Just a minute, please. Let me try to find this. Page 2, section 4. It says here that enormous assistance was given by the civilian police in matters connected with reinforcement and the deployment of personnel. Does the civilian police take part in mobilisation matters in any way?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago how mobilisation is supposed to be taken -- is supposed to take place. The civilian police, as a civilian authority, has no role whatsoever in the implementation of mobilisation. Only after certain deadlines by which conscripts are supposed to report at a certain place, certain authorities can take action vis-a-vis persons who did not report to a given place and there are specific regulations governing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is that to say that the civilian police was actually involved in bringing people in de facto?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This document, could you look at -- I don't have any numbers of these pages. Could you look at where it says, "Darko"?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what does this mean when it says, "Deployed with Darko"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know what unit that is that belongs to the Viteska Brigade, that it would be called the -- the unit at Darko's, or at the cinema or wherever. What kind of units are these? This doesn't exist. There are squads, platoons, companies, et cetera, and also, a unit called work duty. I'm not aware of that. Or a unit at Darko's. I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this paper shows that it was obviously a total improvisation on one side?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does that also mean that this is a very unsystematic paper?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Also, when analysing these names we realised that there are over 30 names that are repeated two times or more; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: That actually confirms that this was done in an improvised fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say that some people were gotten hold of twice and sent somewhere?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, the same men on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And now we shall speed things up a bit. Tell me, these people who were sent to the frontline in such a way, were they capable of participating in combat action when they arrived in these frontlines in such a way? Because you saw who were the people on these lists.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: These were people who did not have any preparation whatsoever, any training whatsoever, any weapons, ammunition. They were taken to the frontline in such a way that they were incapable of any combat action. At that frontline they simply tried to save their bare lives. They would stick their heads into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does a trained soldier have to undergo certain training, individual, tactical, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Absolutely. It is inconceivable to take a person to train -- for shooting, for example, if this person was not trained how to use the weapons that he's going to use. I'm talking about exercises now. I'm talking about training. In order to be able to take part in such exercises, a man has to be totally prepared. That is to say, he has to be familiarised with the weapons concerned. He has to be trained to use the weapons concerned. As far as combat action is concerned, every individual had to go through individual training, group training, squad training, et cetera, depending on the formation in which he was supposed to function, tactical training in order to be able to go to the frontline. I shall say that none of these men -- well, perhaps not none of them but a vast majority of these men did not go through any kind of training in order to be prepared to go to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And tell me, military action, which is highly coordinated, organised, in which several military units take part, can such people be the protagonists of something like this?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was the training of the village guard in any way under your jurisdiction at this time when you were in the Blaskic command? Well, you came to the Vitez Brigade command later, so do you have any information that there was any training of the village guards?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: No. There was nobody able to carry out this training with any kind of quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Later, when the war started, who carried out these attacks that you said required trained soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: These attack operations were not really attack operations, it was just active defence. These actions were mostly carried out by members of Special Purpose Units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So members of the Vitez brigades were usually on the frontlines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Members of the Vitez Brigade, until the end of the war practically, did not carry out a single attack operation. This was all just defence on the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what was the first attack action that was carried out by the Vitez Brigade? When were they capable to carry it out themselves without any Special Purpose Units?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, the first and the only action where only members of the Vitez Brigade units participated occurred towards the end of the war, towards the end of the war, so it was in the liberation of Buhine Kuce. This was carried out by members of the Viteska Brigade without the presence of the Special Purpose Units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This happened in '94?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, this was in '94, towards the end of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The Special Purpose Units that you mentioned which you said were the only ones that were capable of carrying out the attack operations, which units were these? Would you please tell us the names?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: These were Vitezovi, Tvrtkovci, Munje, Skakavci, Lako Jurisna, the Light Charge, also units of the military police, and also some others that I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the difference between the Viteska Brigade, or members of the Vitez Brigade and the units -- Special Purpose Units or the persons who were members of these Special Purpose Units?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: The special purpose units recruited military conscripts who had already been through some training or through some combat. So those who had already been in Jajce, Turbe, Vlasic, these were the -- these -- this was the make-up of these Special Purpose Units. The Vitez Brigade was formed later from the members of these village guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any difference between the way the members of the Vitez Brigade were armed and the members of the Special Purpose Units were armed?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. The Special Purpose Units were well-armed and well-equipped. They had good equipment and good logistics, good material, as opposed to members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Under whose command were these Special Purpose Units? Were they under the command of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not. I don't know who was in command of these units, of these Special Purpose Units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So most of them were outside of the military structure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could the usher please show the witness document 343? Would you please look at the second -- item 2 of this order of the 16th of January of '93? This is an order of Colonel Blaskic. Item 2. Is item 2 in any way talking about an announcement of mobilisation or in any way does it mention mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I don't know what this point is doing in the order by Colonel Blaskic, because this is not in the jurisdiction of a commander of an Operative Zone, to include in HVO formations all unarmed members of the Croatian people. This can only be done by the defence office of the municipality of Vitez based on the defence order of Travnik, and that can be only based on instructions from Mostar. So this order is not -- cannot be carried out, because a commander of a brigade cannot include unarmed civilian members in the HVO structures without the participation of the defence -- Civil Defence office. So this is some kind of a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we're talking about this document, this document has been giving me trouble for some time. The witness has read the same thing that I read, that this is talking about the unarmed. Some colleagues read it as "armed", and the English text says, "armed population." So since there are differences between the original in the Croatian, there are possibilities to read differently this letter "E" or "A" so you would have armed and unarmed. I think we need to get a document where it would be clear exactly what it states. This has been giving me some trouble for some time, and now that this document is being shown to the witness, I think this is the proper time to mention this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if the Prosecutor has got a better copy or the original of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will try to look for it. The only thing I would like to say is that if according to Mr. Radovic there is a translation mistake, I find it a bit awkward. But if it were a mistake, it would mean that the original order written by Mr. Blaskic would have incorporated in the HVO units some unarmed people, which doesn't make any sense at all. I think the English translation which we have is the only reasonable and sensible translation, but of course, I'm not an expert in BCS. Of course, we'll check and make sure that this translation is faithful to the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but what is important is to get another document where the word appears clearly, where we can be sure about what was said in the original. What we're asking is not for you to check the translation, what we're asking you for is to give us a more readable and clear document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We will try to find such a document, Your Honour. We will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody is questioning the quality of the translation, we're just questioning what is stated in Croatian or Serbian -- I mean, Croatian, because one word excludes the other. So there is only one letter which could give a completely different meaning to the words. I asked my colleagues, some read "armed" and some read it as "unarmed". But there is some sense in mobilising unarmed people, because they could have been armed from the -- from some supplies that the brigade had. So not all people had to report to the brigade with arms. So both of these things make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I asked the Prosecution to try to provide a better copy of the original. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So according to regulations which were in force at that time, such a mobilisation order could not have been issued by the commander of the Operative Zone but exclusively by the defence office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is a kind of declaratory order that has no weight because it cannot be implemented in this way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One more question concerning this document. At that time were you in the command? Do you know whether any kind of mobilisation was being carried out at that time?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: During the whole time, so until this date, everything that we were doing, all of our work, was directed towards the army of Republika Srpska. Colonel Blaskic insisted on the lines towards the army of Republika Srpska. He -- there was no need for him to deal with the BH army. Of course we monitored the situation on the ground, and on one occasion, at a morning briefing, we suggested that we were not happy with the deployment of the units of the BH army, and then he told us, he gave us an assignment, my colleague Ivica Cubanac, who was one of the section heads, for him to locate the units of the BH army on the map at that time. Then we reached some -- we kind of came to some illogical situations regarding this deployment, the way the units were deployed. The units of the BH army were not always such that they were turned against the army of Republika Srpska. So at that time it was very strange to us that he had formed a training centre in Kruscica, for example, for soldiers who were mostly from Krajina. Then he also had a large military centre in Preocica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You're talking about the BH army?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right, the BH army. So in Han Bila and so on. So this wasn't quite clear to us, this deployment of soldiers. So we drew attention to the fact that this wasn't okay. Up until then he would always say that the BH army is our ally, that we were dealing with the same tasks, and that was to defend ourselves from the aggression of the army of Republika Srpska. So all his commands were towards calming the situation with the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't directly ask you that, but you said that well. I was really asking you if you knew whether at the time that you were at the headquarters of the Operative Zone, whether any kind of mobilisation of Croat population was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I am not aware that any mobilisation like that was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution document 341 and 342 very quickly? This is the document which is a decision on the -- decree on the structuring of the home guard. Do you know whether this order on the structure of the home guard in the region of the Vitez municipality was ever implemented? So based on this decree, was any kind of home guard unit established before the end of -- before the start of the war?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The first home guard units were formed after the war. This is the 92nd Home Guard Regiment. Before that, no unit was formed that would be a home guard unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this other document, which is order 399/93, which states that a temporary home guard command was being formed in the municipality and three men were being proposed. Item 2 says that, "In view of the fact that there were such facilities of special importance in the Vitez municipality, we recommend that a company be formed." This is a document from March 12th, 1993. So do you know whether, at least on paper, any kind of home guard company was formed in March or April of '93?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, I don't have that document in front of me, but I know for a fact that in that period not a single home guard unit was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would mobilisation be carried out in the way stated and described in document 335, which we looked at just now? Would -- had these home guard units been formed?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, it would be logical that they would have been formed -- if they had been formed, they would have simply been deployed to the frontline and people would not have been collected in this way. If there had been a home guard unit, it would simply have been called to that line of defence, and if I can comment on this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: What does that say? It doesn't say anything to me. It would be logical for a command to be formed, a command of the home guard unit, any kind of size, which would later appoint the command staff, and only after that would it go about calling up of home guard soldiers. So this is just an order of a commander for company -- home guard companies. But then in this item 2 they say that they recommend that one company be formed, so this doesn't say anything to me. It means that it was probably never implemented. So this really -- this document really has no importance, it has no value.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One more question. According to the rules of military service, according to certain customs that were accepted by soldiers, commanders of individual units, tell me, was it customary to send into an attack that was a high risk attack the members of the same family?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: My commander and all commanders of lower units had instructions to send, whenever possible, or, rather, not to send, whenever possible, two brothers or a father and a son to the same frontline, unless they specifically had requested that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So they were not even sent to the frontline itself, let alone into an attack?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me something else. You know Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, do you?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And, tell me, what kind of people are they?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I've known Zoran for a longer period of time, Mirjan somewhat less. I consider them to be good friends, good colleagues at work, good fathers. They are good men, as we say, and I would really be proud if someone would say of me, or of my own child, that he were a good man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rajic. I have completed my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any examination-in-chief by Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were good men. On the basis of which elements from your life do you draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I already said that I knew Zoran longer. We worked in the same organisation, we cooperated at work, so that part of our lives was always based on a fair relationship, and it was always improving. I also knew him personally. Zoran was a member of a folklore society. He was a man who worked with children. We were happy to send our children to a society that promoted a healthy life, that we wanted to keep our children off the streets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you are talking about Zoran, right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, I am talking about Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mention Mirjan too.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I want to talk about them separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can speak about each and every one separately. Because you know Zoran better, right?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I wanted to speak in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now Mirjan.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Well, often we would sit together and play the accordion and sing. He is a quiet man, a vivacious person, a man who likes people and likes to make other people happy. That is my impression of him. He worked hard at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, at work, and in this cultural society, how does Zoran and Mirjan behave to members of other ethnic groups, because in the area of Vitez there were Serbs and Muslims as well? Tell me, did he take a different attitude towards people belonging to other ethnic or religious groups, I don't even know what to say any more, whether he in any way behaved differently towards Muslims and whatever.

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: Now you are asking me about something that I and they never thought about at that time. When we danced folk dances together, when we watched these people performing, I just knew that Zoran and Mirjan and others were dancing. And I, just as they did, we never really distinguished between the people in the colour, whether it was a Serb or a Croat or whoever dancing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after the elections, when the national parties won a majority, were any attempts made to break up this cultural society, where they danced, and to create separate cultural societies?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, to the best of your knowledge, as far as the Kupreskic brothers are concerned, do you believe or, rather, what kind of people are they? Could they kill others, could they slaughter others, could they kill children and do things like that?

utterances.speaker: Mario Rajic
utterances.text: It is my deep conviction that they couldn't possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Since it is clear that we can't get through with this witness today -- I would like to ask Counsel Pavkovic whether there are other Defence counsel willing to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No. The other Defence counsel do not intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor, how much time do you need? Do you think you could finish your cross-examination in -- no, we can't, seven minutes. Then there would be re-examination, in any case, by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Seven minutes would not be enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will resume proceedings on the 8th of February, Monday, the 8th of February at 9.00 sharp, and with Mr. Rajic as a witness. So we adjourn our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
